newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori to discuss differences with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori to discuss differences with Japan.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori left on Friday for a summit in Canada with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to discuss differences over negotiations with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages for the 45th day.

Ahead of Saturday's meeting in Toronto, a Japanese government source said Tokyo and Lima were divided over whether the time had come to give ground on the rebels' main demand that Peru free hundreds of their jailed comrades.

Negotiations with the roughly 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holed up at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima have been deadlocked for weeks because Fujimori refused to discuss the demand.

"We are worried that there could be an unexpected development. Direct negotiations must be held soon," the Tokyo source said. Hashimoto would urge Fujimori to soften his position to allow the rebels' demand on the talks agenda, he added.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo, Interior Minister Juan Briones Davila and several government party legislators, including congressional president Joy Way accompanied Fujimori.

Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canada's ambasssador to Peru, Anthony Vincent -- two members of a commission set to supervise talks between the government and rebels -- also traveled to Canada. The Red Cross -- the final member of the commission -- did not send a representataive to the meeting.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said his country was chosen to host Saturday's meeting because of its mediating role in the crisis.
Tokyo also criticized Peru for endangering the lives of hostages -- including about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen -- with its increasingly bold police tactics at the site.
Hashimoto, who left Tokyo on Friday, called several times this week for Fujimori to exercise caution to prevent "accidents or incidents."
Before leaving for Toronto Fujimori sought to defuse tensions between the two governments by admitting stricter orders to police officers were needed.
He told Argentina's CVN television network obscene gestures by police that provoked the rebels earlier this week to fire several shots at the officers "were not planned."
However, a senior Peruvian government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, insisted Fujimori would not apologize to Hashimoto for the provocative police moves.

The summit, which could be preceded with an informal meeting, was aimed at achieving "a very close coordination," according to Fujimori. "If we were in an emergency situation we would need to be in close contact," he said.
But Fujimori would not use the meeting to seek approval for a military assault on the mined and booby-trapped compound, the Peruvian government source said.
Hashimoto said on Thursday the weekend summit would confirm Tokyo and Lima's joint strategy of not "caving in to terrorism."

Fujimori said he was prepared for the six-week-old siege to drag on. "It could go on a lot longer still. I am patient (to wait) for the hostages to be freed safe and sound ... It could take some weeks, some months," Fujimori said.

Returning from Canada, Fujimori will travel to Washington on Sunday for a meeting on Monday with U.S. President Bill Clinton to thank him for Washington's strong backing during the crisis, government sources said.
Washington did not, however, confirm the meeting and Fujimori said it was not formally scheduled.

Police repeated on Friday their tactics aimed at wearing down the rebels by blasting in the early hours broadcasts of martial music, sirens and the roar of aircraft at the building. Just before dawn they played a reveille.
A twin-engine military plane also flew slowly over the site.

The MRTA rebels seized hundreds of guests when they stormed the residence Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception. They released most of the captives but kept those they considered the most important bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, top government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and the Japanese.
